meta.description: Not Douglas Adams. Lewis Thomas wrote it in The Lives of a Cell (1974); the famous wording is Carl Sagan's 1978 paraphrase in Murmurs of Earth.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I would send the complete works of Johann Sebastian Bach, but that would be boasting'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Douglas Adams, and not quite Carl Sagan. The line traces to biologist Lewis Thomas, 1974 — but the famous wording is Sagan's paraphrase of him.

answer.label: Not Douglas Adams — actually Lewis Thomas
answer.authorDates: 1913–1993 · American physician, biologist and essayist; president of the Sloan-Kettering Institute
answer.sourceLine: Douglas Adams never said it. The thought belongs to the physician-essayist Lewis Thomas, who wrote in The Lives of a Cell (1974) that the first message humanity sent into space should be music: “I would vote for Bach, all of Bach, streamed out into space, over and over again. We would be bragging, of course.” The neater sentence everyone quotes — “the complete works … but that would be boasting” — is Carl Sagan’s rendering of a spoken Thomas remark, published in Murmurs of Earth (1978) and credited to Thomas by name.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Lives of a Cell: Notes of a Biology Watcher
Carl Sagan et al., Murmurs of Earth: The Voyager Interstellar Record (Random House, 1978), page 13
Genuine thought, paraphrased wording — and the wrong author on the label

source.excerpt: Perhaps the safest thing to do at the outset, if technology permits, is to send music. This language may be the best we have for explaining what we are like to others in space, with least ambiguity. I would vote for Bach, all of Bach, streamed out into space, over and over again. We would be bragging, of course, but it is surely excusable for us to put the best possible face on at the beginning of such an acquaintance. We can tell the harder truths later.
trail: 1974 — Lewis Thomas publishes The Lives of a Cell, arguing that the safest opening message to send into space is music, and voting for “all of Bach.” The book goes on to win National Book Awards in two categories. Wikiquote carries the passage, sourced to the 1974 collection ↗

1978 — Carl Sagan’s Murmurs of Earth, the book about the Voyager Golden Record, supplies the wording everyone now quotes — and credits it properly, naming “the biologist Lewis Thomas, president of the Sloan-Kettering Institute” and flagging his own version as “words to this effect.” Quote Investigator transcribes the page ↗

1996–2007 — the name falls off. An obituary of Sagan quotes the line from an unnamed “biologist”; Stephen Fry credits Sagan on QI; then a forum post hands it to Douglas Adams. All three steps are documented and dated ↗

Meanwhile — three Bach selections really did fly, more than any other composer on the record: a Brandenburg Concerto movement, a violin gavotte, and a prelude and fugue played by Glenn Gould. Beethoven, the runner-up, got two. The full track list ↗
source.excerptNote: Notice what is not in the original: no “complete works,” no “boasting,” and “I would vote for” rather than “I would send.” The famous sentence is Sagan’s 1978 rendering of something Thomas said aloud, not of this written passage. (Quote Investigator places these lines on page 45, in the essay “Ceti”; Wikiquote files the identical passage under “Vibes.” Only Quote Investigator gives a page number and claims verification against scans, so that is the citation used here.)

author.name: Lewis Thomas
author.kicker: The man who actually said it
author.heading: Who was Lewis Thomas?
author.metaLine: 1913–1993 · American physician and biologist · president of the Sloan-Kettering Institute
author.bio: Lewis Thomas was an American physician and biologist who doubled as one of the finest essayists of his generation — his encyclopedia entry needs eight nouns to cover him, among them poet, etymologist, administrator and educator. He served as president of the Sloan-Kettering Institute in New York, and his 1974 collection The Lives of a Cell: Notes of a Biology Watcher won National Book Awards in two separate categories, Arts and Letters and the Sciences. He wrote about biology the way a good host talks at dinner: warmly, briefly, and with the confidence to make a joke at the species’ expense.

We would be bragging, of course" in The Lives of a Cell: Notes of a Biology Watcher (New York: Viking Press, 1974), 45. The familiar wording — "I would send the complete works of Johann Sebastian Bach … But that … would be boasting" — is Carl Sagan's paraphrase of a spoken Thomas remark in Murmurs of Earth: The Voyager Interstellar Record (New York: Random House, 1978), 13. misattribution.heading: Four names, one remark
misattribution.intro: This is an unusually crowded misattribution: Quote Investigator opens its investigation by listing four candidate speakers. Only one of them said it, and even he did not say it in these words.

items.why: Quote Investigator’s verdict is blunt: “Douglas Adams praised the music of Bach, but he did not make the statement under examination.” The earliest Adams credit it could document is a 2007 post on a trumpet players’ forum — more than thirty years after Thomas wrote the line. Adams was a real Bach enthusiast, which is likely why the credit stuck: he wrote a newspaper appreciation of the Brandenburg Concertos in 1999 containing the line “Bach tells you what it’s like to be the universe.” That is his. This one is not. Quote Investigator’s findings ↗ Worth noting too: Wikiquote’s Douglas Adams page ↗ runs to roughly 38,000 characters and contains no Bach quotation whatsoever.

Sagan is the reason the pithy version exists, but he never claimed it. In Murmurs of Earth he introduces it as “an earlier remark of the biologist Lewis Thomas” and marks his own phrasing as approximate. Stephen Fry nonetheless credited Sagan for it on an episode of the BBC panel show QI in 2004, in the variant “I think that would just be showing off.” Both citations are dated at Quote Investigator ↗

Thomas is the right author of the idea, and the quotable sentence is a fair summary of him. It is still not a sentence he is documented as writing. What he wrote was “I would vote for Bach, all of Bach, streamed out into space, over and over again. We would be bragging, of course.” Sagan compressed a spoken version into “the complete works … but that would be boasting,” and that compression is what travelled. Wikiquote’s sourced text of the original ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The joke is Lewis Thomas’s, the phrasing is Carl Sagan’s, and Douglas Adams simply had the misfortune of being famous, funny and fond of Bach. Quote Investigator, 12 March 2024 ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: When Thomas wrote this, the Voyager probes had not yet launched. He was thinking about a colder problem — the conference-room question of what electromagnetic message humanity should beam at a civilisation that might be a century or more away, and might not reply for two hundred years. His answer was that anything we said about ourselves in words would embarrass us by the time it arrived, and that music was the one language likely to survive the trip with its meaning intact.

The joke lands because it concedes the whole game in half a sentence. Sending all of Bach is an act of self-flattery, and Thomas knows it, and does it anyway — “it is surely excusable for us to put the best possible face on at the beginning of such an acquaintance. We can tell the harder truths later.” That last clause is the part nobody quotes, and it is the part that makes the line more than a quip.
context.detailsSummary: What actually went on the record
detailsBody: Thomas did not get the complete works. When the Golden Record was assembled for the two Voyager probes launched in 1977, Bach got three slots: the first movement of the Brandenburg Concerto No. 2 with the Munich Bach Orchestra under Karl Richter, the Gavotte en Rondeau from the Partita for Solo Violin No. 3 played by Arthur Grumiaux, and the Prelude and Fugue in C from Book II of the Well-Tempered Clavier played by Glenn Gould.

That is more than any other composer — Beethoven, next in line, got two. So Thomas lost the argument on volume, in the sense that nobody was ever going to fit the complete works onto a twelve-inch disc, and won it on every other count: Bach is the most-represented composer up there. The remark, meanwhile, outlived the debate by being repeatedly handed to the wrong person.
context.pull: We would be bragging, of course, but it is surely excusable for us to put the best possible face on at the beginning of such an acquaintance.

sourcesVerified.claim: Lewis Thomas originated the remark in The Lives of a Cell (Viking Press, 1974), page 45, essay "Ceti": "I would vote for Bach, all of Bach, streamed out into space, over and over again. We would be bragging, of course, but it is surely excusable for us to put the best possible face on at the beginning of such an acquaintance. We can tell the harder truths later." The popular wording is Carl Sagan's paraphrase in Murmurs of Earth (Random House, 1978), page 13, where Sagan names Thomas and marks it "words to this effect." QI concludes: "Douglas Adams praised the music of Bach, but he did not make the statement under examination." Also documents the 1996 Independent obituary ("a biologist"), Stephen Fry crediting Sagan on QI in 2004, and a 2007 Trumpet Herald Forum post crediting Adams; and Adams's own 1999 Guardian piece on the Brandenburg Concertos.

Wikiquote's Lewis Thomas page carries the passage "Perhaps the safest thing to do at the outset, if technology permits, is to send music... I would vote for Bach, all of Bach, streamed out into space, over and over again. We would be bragging of course..." sourced to The Lives of a Cell: Notes of a Biology Watcher (1974), where it is filed under the essay "Vibes" with no page number. Verified by fetching this page's own raw wikitext via ?action=raw.

Wikiquote's Douglas Adams page (38,328 bytes of wikitext) contains no Bach quotation and no occurrence of "boast" or "bragg" anywhere; its only top-level sections are Quotes, Quotes about Adams, and External links. Verified by grepping this page's own raw wikitext via ?action=raw — zero hits.

The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of The lives of a cell; notes of a biology watcher by Thomas, Lewis, 1913-1993, dated 1974, published New York, Viking Press — matching the edition Quote Investigator cites. Edition, creator, date and publisher confirmed via https://archive.org/metadata/livesofcellnotes00thomrich; the details page returns HTTP 200.

The Internet Archive holds a scan of Murmurs of Earth: the Voyager interstellar record with publisher "New York : Random House", date 1978, ISBN 0394410475 — the Random House first edition Quote Investigator cites for page 13. Edition, date and publisher confirmed via https://archive.org/metadata/murmursofearthvo0000unse; details page returns HTTP 200, borrow-only (access-restricted-item true). The Archive's other copy, murmursofearthvo00saga, is the 1979 Ballantine Books paperback reprint (ISBN 0345283961) and is deliberately NOT linked, because its pagination differs from the cited first edition.

The Voyager Golden Record music list includes exactly three Bach entries — Brandenburg Concerto No. 2 in F Major, BWV 1047: I. Allegro (Munich Bach Orchestra / Karl Richter, 4:40); Partita for Violin Solo No. 3 in E Major, BWV 1006: III. Gavotte en Rondeau (Arthur Grumiaux, 2:55); and The Well-Tempered Clavier, Book II, Prelude and Fugue in C major, BWV 870 (Glenn Gould, 4:48). Bach is the most-represented composer on the record: Beethoven, the runner-up, has exactly two entries — Symphony No. 5 in C minor, Opus 67: I. Allegro con brio, and String Quartet No. 13 in B-flat major, Opus 130: V. Cavatina. No other composer appears more than twice. Re-verified against the linked track table on 9 Sep 2026, correcting an earlier reading of this same page that credited Beethoven with three.

Lewis Thomas lived 25 November 1913 to 3 December 1993, was an American physician, poet, etymologist, essayist, administrator, educator, policy advisor and biologist, served as President of Memorial Sloan-Kettering Institute, and his The Lives of a Cell: Notes of a Biology Watcher (Viking Press, 1974) won National Book Awards in two categories, Arts and Letters and the Sciences.
